job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Thornby, above my dad's heating and plumbing workshop. I'm up at six like the rest of the family. I help Dad load the van in the morning when he's short-handed, then I come back and do my applications at the workshop's office computer. Sundays are church and a long lunch with my grandparents. I don't use AI tools, I've never seen the point, and I'd rather write my own emails.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. Tell me about your degree and your internship.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electronic engineering at Garrow University, and my final project was a controller for a greenhouse heater that Dad's customers could actually fit. My internship was six weeks at a firm that makes alarm systems, testing circuit boards on the bench. What I'm after is a steady engineering job with a firm that's been around forty years and trains its young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I thought so. There's a lot of noise about it. Noise doesn't build a house, and real work still needs real people. I'd tell my friends at church so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still waiting for my first offer, and that sits with me. There are plenty of firms around Thornby, but they want someone with a couple of years behind them. My dad says it took him eighteen months to find his first proper position, and that helps a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and I'd go in person to the smaller firms, with a printed CV and my greenhouse controller in a box. I'd ask my dad's customers if they know of engineering firms. And I'd help in the workshop in between, because I'd rather be useful than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My family's good about it, but I don't like being the one at the kitchen table in the middle of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go in person with the controller. Has that worked before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once. A man at a small firm looked at it for ten minutes and asked good questions. He didn't have a job, but he gave me a name, and I'll take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your father feel about you working in the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's pleased, though he says I'm an engineer and shouldn't be fixing boilers. I tell him it's engineering with oil on your hands.

I'd tell friends at church that real work still needs real people.

feel: **Uneasy**: my family's good about it, but I dislike being at the kitchen table midday.

fieldNote: Takes comfort in his **father's** own slow start.
Prefers in-person **approaches** and physical proof of his work.
Sees **workshop** help as useful, not a step down.

steps.text: Visit small engineering firms in person with a printed CV
Show the greenhouse controller to Dad's customers
Help in Dad's workshop two days a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of fuss, but I'd also say firms should keep training young people and not just buy software. I'd tell my pastor that this is a test of whether we look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think circuit design and testing, my kind of entry work, partly goes to software. Hands-on bench work still needs people, but the design desk shrinks. I'd be one of many young engineers fighting for fewer places, and I don't use the tools that would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to firms with workshops and testing rooms. I'd go to the local engineering institution's evening and I'd ask about apprenticeships, even if it's a step back. And I'd learn one of these tools slowly, but only if my future boss tells me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got family and money behind me, but it still feels like a closing door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn a tool only if your boss tells you to. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust my own judgement on which one's worth the time, and I don't want to be known as the new boy who plays with gadgets. Once someone I respect says use this, I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would apprenticeship mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less pay for a couple of years, but you learn the trade properly, with someone older looking over your shoulder. I'd do it, and I wouldn't be embarrassed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a terrible idea and I'd say so plainly. I'd tell people that nobody voted for this, and that governments must slow it until families can cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm alarmed. Everything I've trained for is thinking work, and it would be done cheaper before I've even had a full-time job. Dad's work, hands-on heating jobs, has about three more years than mine, but a quarter of his customers' jobs would be at risk too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever job comes first, and I'd give Dad my full week in the workshop and learn his trade for real. I'd put my savings in cash and give my mother a bit more for the household. I'd also go to church more, to be around people who'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep badly, and I'd hide it from my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hide it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mum would worry more, and Dad would say he should've pushed me into the trade at sixteen. I don't want him blaming himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by nobody voted for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies are doing this to everyone, and nobody asked ordinary people. If a government can't slow something down that affects everyone's wage, what is it for?

think: Everything I've trained for is thinking work, done **cheaper** before I've had a full-time job.
Dad's heating work has about **three more years**, but his customers are at risk too.

fieldNote: Anger at companies and **government** covers a fear he keeps from his parents.

steps.text: Take the first engineering or technician job that comes

Lean on church friends and family for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more like it. I'd say that families and churches should be helping young people find proper trades and work now, not waiting for politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me five years is workable. I'd get a first job, I'd get a few years of experience, and I'd learn a trade on the side. By 2031 I'd have something solid. Still, thinking AI is the first to move, so my desk work is the weaker part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get hired in a workshop or testing role, and work evenings and weekends with Dad. I'd save two-thirds of my pay and I'd look at buying a part of the workshop one day. I'd also start courting seriously, to be honest, because I'd want a family settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. There's a way through, and I know my people would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said courting seriously. How does the timeline affect that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I know the next five years are shaky, I'd want someone with me, not on my own. I'd also want to save for a deposit, so the sooner I'm in work the better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from a first employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who says honestly if the job is secure, and gives me someone to learn from. A firm that treats you as an apprentice and not a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a good stretch. I'd say people should use it to build things and families, not to panic, and that firms should keep taking on young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's calm, mostly. I'd have a decade of work, probably a family, and maybe part of the workshop. Thinking work will change, and I'd have to learn something new, but I'd have time and people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, put in the years and stay close to church and family. I'd learn the new tools when everyone else has, around year three or four, and I'd use them to run the workshop's quotes and orders. I'd save for a house and put a bit away for my own children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A steady life is what I'm after, and this one leaves room for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said learn the tools around year three or four. Why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then they'll be dull and settled, and everyone will know the mistakes. I'd rather learn from other people's mistakes than make my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to pass on to your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you can do honest work with your hands and your head, and that you can rely on your family. The details change but that doesn't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. A lot of what I believe in is slow: earning your place, learning from older people, building things that last. Two years doesn't leave room for that. What would help is employers who keep hiring and training young people, and families who can keep us afloat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the loud people on screens don't speak for people like me. Plenty of us just want an honest job, a family and a bit of respect.

headlineQuote: Plenty of us just want an honest job, a family and a bit of respect.
portrait: Liam is a **23-year-old** electronic engineering graduate living above his father's heating workshop, still without an offer after several months.
He is **traditional** and favours work, apprenticeships and family support over handouts, and he trusts firms that train their own people.
He **never uses AI tools** and prefers the familiar, so he moves slowly and leans on family and church.
His mood is **uneasy** or anxious in most scenarios and alarmed in the 2028 world, where slow, earned careers have no room.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because earning your place and learning from older people takes time he would not have.
whatWouldHelp: Employers that keep **hiring and training** young people, and **family** that can keep them afloat.
